subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — Ratio Analysis and Interpretation
content:
RATIO ANALYSIS

Ratios convert accounting figures into relationships that can be compared across years, businesses or targets. A ratio is useful only when interpreted in context.

PROFITABILITY RATIOS

Gross profit margin
= Gross profit / Revenue × 100

It indicates the proportion of revenue remaining after cost of sales. A fall may arise from lower selling prices, higher purchase/production costs, discounts or changes in product mix.

Net profit margin
= Net profit / Revenue × 100

It indicates how much profit is generated from each unit of revenue after relevant expenses.

Return on capital employed (ROCE)
= Operating profit / Capital employed × 100
where the exact profit and capital definitions should follow the question's convention.

Return on assets
= Relevant profit / Relevant asset base × 100, using the convention specified.

Operating expenses to sales
= Operating expenses / Revenue × 100.

LIQUIDITY RATIOS

Current ratio
= Current assets / Current liabilities.

Quick ratio
= (Current assets − inventory) / Current liabilities
or the equivalent quick-assets formulation required.

A high current ratio is not automatically good: excessive idle inventory or receivables can indicate inefficient resource use.

Receivables collection period
= Trade receivables / Credit sales × 365 days.

Payables payment period
= Trade payables / Credit purchases × 365 days.

Inventory turnover
= Cost of sales / Average inventory
where average inventory is normally (opening + closing inventory)/2 if appropriate.

RESOURCE UTILISATION

Total assets turnover
= Revenue / Capital employed or total assets according to the stated convention.

Non-current assets turnover
= Revenue / Non-current assets.

Current assets turnover
= Revenue / Current assets.

Capital employed turnover
= Revenue / Capital employed.

INVESTMENT RATIOS

Earnings per share (EPS)
= Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders / weighted average ordinary shares.

Price earnings ratio (P/E)
= Market price per share / EPS.

Dividend yield
= Dividend per share / Market price per share × 100.

Dividend cover
= Earnings per share / Dividend per share.

GEARING AND CAPITAL STRUCTURE

Debt-to-equity ratio compares debt financing with equity financing.

Gearing indicates the extent to which a business uses debt relative to equity/capital. Higher gearing can increase financial risk because interest and repayment obligations remain even when profits fall.

INTERPRETING RATIOS

Always:
1. calculate correctly;
2. compare with previous period or benchmark;
3. identify the direction of change;
4. explain possible causes;
5. state implications;
6. suggest appropriate action where requested.

Example:
If gross margin falls from 35% to 28%, possible causes include rising input costs, lower selling prices, increased discounts or an adverse product mix. Management should investigate purchasing costs, pricing and product profitability rather than assuming the cause.

LIMITATIONS
Ratios:
• use historical data;
• can be distorted by accounting policies;
• may be affected by inflation;
• may be difficult to compare businesses with different sizes or structures;
• can hide absolute changes;
• depend on reliable underlying figures.

A strong evaluation combines ratios with cash-flow information, budgets, industry conditions and qualitative evidence.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — Cost Accounting: Cost Terms, Cost Classification and Absorption Costing
content:
COST ACCOUNTING

Cost accounting identifies, classifies, measures and analyses costs for products, services, jobs and activities. It supports pricing, planning, control and decision making.

COST UNIT
A cost unit is a unit of product or service for which costs are measured, such as one tonne, one unit produced, one passenger-kilometre or one job.

COST CENTRE
A cost centre is a location, department, function or activity for which costs are collected and analysed.

COST CODING
Cost codes are identifiers used to classify and trace costs consistently.

PERIOD COST VS PRODUCT COST
Product costs are attached to production/inventory under the relevant costing system until recognised as expense.
Period costs are charged to the period in which they arise.

RELEVANT VS IRRELEVANT COSTS
A relevant cost is a future cost that differs between alternatives.
An irrelevant cost does not change between alternatives or has already been incurred.

OPPORTUNITY COST
The benefit sacrificed by choosing one alternative instead of the next best alternative.

SUNK COST
A past cost that cannot be changed by a current decision. It should not normally influence a decision except where the question specifically requires consideration of historical information for another purpose.

COST BEHAVIOUR
Fixed cost: remains constant in total over a relevant activity range, although fixed cost per unit changes with volume.
Variable cost: changes in total with activity; unit variable cost may remain constant over a relevant range.
Semi-variable cost: contains fixed and variable components.
Semi-fixed/step cost: remains fixed over a range and then changes when activity crosses a threshold.

ABSORPTION COSTING

Absorption costing assigns production overheads to units of output.

OVERHEAD APPORTIONMENT
Apportion common costs among cost centres using an appropriate basis.

ALLOCATION
Charging an entire cost to a cost centre when the cost is directly attributable to that centre.

APPORTIONMENT
Dividing a common cost among cost centres using a rational basis.

ABSORPTION
Charging overhead from production cost centres to units/jobs.

OVERHEAD ABSORPTION RATE (OAR)
OAR = Budgeted overhead / Budgeted activity.

Activity could be labour hours, machine hours, units or another suitable base.

OVER/UNDER ABSORPTION
Absorbed overhead = OAR × actual activity.
If absorbed overhead > actual overhead incurred → over-absorption.
If absorbed overhead < actual overhead incurred → under-absorption.

COST SHEET
A cost sheet may show:
Direct materials
+ direct labour
+ direct expenses
= prime cost
+ production overhead
= production cost
+ appropriate non-production costs
= total cost
+ profit
= sales value.

The exact presentation depends on the question.

ADVANTAGES OF ABSORPTION COSTING
• full production cost is assigned to output;
• useful for inventory valuation under applicable financial reporting requirements;
• can support long-term pricing decisions.

LIMITATIONS
• overhead allocation can be arbitrary;
• unit costs can change because of volume changes;
• may be less useful for short-term decisions where fixed costs do not change.

CLOSING INVENTORY
Under absorption costing, closing inventory generally contains an allocated share of production fixed overhead. This creates a key difference from marginal costing.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — Marginal Costing, Contribution and Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis
content:
MARGINAL COSTING

Marginal costing separates variable costs from fixed costs. The central measure is contribution.

Contribution = Sales − Variable cost.

Contribution per unit = Selling price per unit − Variable cost per unit.

Total contribution = Contribution per unit × units sold.

Profit = Total contribution − Fixed costs.

BREAK-EVEN POINT

Break-even units
= Fixed costs / Contribution per unit.

Break-even sales value
= Fixed costs / Contribution-to-sales ratio.

CONTRIBUTION-TO-SALES RATIO (C/S RATIO)
= Contribution / Sales × 100.

MARGIN OF SAFETY
Margin of safety = Actual or budgeted sales − Break-even sales.

It can be expressed in units, value or percentage.

A larger positive margin of safety generally means a greater buffer before the business reaches break-even.

COST-VOLUME-PROFIT ANALYSIS
CVP analysis studies how selling price, variable cost, fixed cost and volume interact to affect profit.

Target profit units:
(Fixed costs + target profit) / contribution per unit.

If selling price or variable cost changes, contribution changes and the break-even point changes.

SHORT-RUN DECISION MAKING

Where spare capacity exists and fixed costs will not change, contribution can be more relevant than full absorption cost for decisions such as:
• accepting a special order;
• choosing between products;
• discontinuing a product;
• using a scarce resource.

However, qualitative factors and long-term effects must be considered.

LIMITING FACTOR
When one resource is scarce, rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource.

Contribution per limiting factor = Unit contribution / Units of scarce resource required per unit.

Choose the combination that maximises total contribution, subject to constraints.

ABSORPTION VS MARGINAL PROFIT

The difference is caused mainly by the treatment of fixed production overhead in inventory.

If inventory increases, absorption costing may report higher profit because some fixed production overhead is carried forward in closing inventory.
If inventory decreases, absorption costing may report lower profit because fixed production overhead released from opening inventory is charged.

RECONCILIATION
A reconciliation statement explains the difference between marginal and absorption profits by using the change in inventory multiplied by the fixed production overhead absorption rate, where the question's assumptions support that method.

EXAMPLE
Selling price = $50
Variable cost = $30
Contribution = $20
Fixed costs = $40,000

Break-even units = 40,000 / 20 = 2,000 units.

At 3,000 units:
Contribution = 3,000 × 20 = $60,000
Profit = $60,000 − $40,000 = $20,000.

If target profit is $30,000:
Required units = (40,000 + 30,000) / 20 = 3,500 units.

EXAM CHECKS
• use contribution, not profit, in short-run contribution calculations;
• state the limiting factor;
• distinguish unit contribution from total contribution;
• check whether fixed costs really remain unchanged;
• do not ignore qualitative factors.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — Job and Batch Costing
content:
JOB COSTING

Job costing determines the cost of an individual job. It is useful where work is customised, such as specialised production, printing, construction or repair work.

ELEMENTS OF JOB COST
Direct materials
+ direct labour
+ direct expenses
+ absorbed overhead
= total job cost.

JOB COSTING PROCESS
1. Identify the job.
2. Record direct materials issued.
3. Record direct labour.
4. Add direct expenses.
5. Apply the appropriate overhead absorption rate.
6. Calculate total cost.
7. Add profit/mark-up if required.
8. Determine selling price.

BATCH COSTING

A batch is a group of identical or similar units produced together.

Batch cost = Total cost of batch.
Unit cost = Total batch cost / Units in batch.

Where overhead is absorbed:
Batch prime cost + absorbed overhead = total batch cost.

If a batch contains 500 units and total batch cost is $12,500:
Unit cost = $12,500 / 500 = $25.

MARK-UP VS MARGIN

Mark-up is profit expressed as a percentage of cost.
Margin is profit expressed as a percentage of sales.

If cost = $80 and mark-up = 25%:
Profit = $20
Selling price = $100.

If margin = 25% and cost = $75:
Selling price = Cost / (1 − margin)
= 75 / 0.75
= $100.

This distinction is a frequent source of errors.

OVERHEAD ABSORPTION IN JOB/BATCH COSTING
If the OAR is $6 per labour hour and Job A uses 40 labour hours:
Overhead absorbed = 6 × 40 = $240.

If direct materials are $900 and direct labour $500:
Prime cost = $1,400.
Total cost after overhead = $1,640.

If required profit is 20% of cost:
Selling price = $1,640 × 1.20 = $1,968.

If required margin is 20% of selling price:
Selling price = $1,640 / 0.80 = $2,050.

JOB SHEET
A job sheet should clearly identify:
• job number;
• customer/description where applicable;
• direct material;
• direct labour;
• direct expenses;
• overhead;
• total cost;
• selling price;
• profit.

EXAM TECHNIQUE
Keep the working in a logical vertical sequence. A marker should be able to see how every figure was obtained.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — Standard Costing and Variance Analysis
content:
STANDARD COSTING

Standard costing establishes expected costs and revenues against which actual performance can be compared.

STANDARD TYPES
Ideal standard: assumes highly efficient conditions with little or no allowance for normal inefficiency.
Basic standard: a long-term benchmark.
Current/attainable standard: reflects realistic operating conditions and expected efficiency.

VARIANCE
Variance = Actual result compared with standard/budget result.

A favourable variance generally improves profit relative to standard; an adverse variance reduces profit. Always state whether the variance is favourable or adverse rather than relying on the sign alone.

MATERIAL VARIANCES

Material price variance:
(Standard price − Actual price) × Actual quantity purchased/used according to the required convention.

Material usage variance:
(Standard quantity for actual output − Actual quantity used) × Standard price.

Interpretation:
Price variance may be caused by supplier price changes, bulk discounts, inflation or purchasing decisions.
Usage variance may arise from waste, quality problems, production efficiency or material substitution.

LABOUR VARIANCES

Labour rate variance:
(Standard rate − Actual rate) × Actual hours worked.

Labour efficiency variance:
(Standard hours for actual output − Actual hours worked) × Standard rate.

Possible causes include overtime premiums, wage changes, training, labour skill mix, downtime and production efficiency.

SALES VARIANCES
Depending on the required syllabus treatment:
Sales price variance compares actual selling price with standard selling price for actual quantity.
Sales volume variance compares actual volume with standard volume using the relevant standard contribution/profit basis.

RECONCILIATION
Variance analysis should reconcile standard/budgeted profit with actual profit:
Standard profit
± relevant favourable/adverse variances
= actual profit.

SIGN CONVENTION
If using:
F = favourable
A = adverse
Then label every variance clearly.

EXAMPLE
Standard material price = $4 per kg
Actual price = $4.50
Actual quantity = 1,000 kg

Price variance = (4.00 − 4.50) × 1,000 = $500 A.

If standard quantity for actual output is 900 kg:
Usage variance = (900 − 1,000) × 4.00 = $400 A.

Total material cost variance = $900 A.

MANAGEMENT USE
Variance analysis is not only about finding blame. It helps identify areas requiring investigation, such as procurement, production methods, quality, staffing, standards and market conditions.

LIMITATIONS
• standards can become outdated;
• responsibility may be shared;
• one favourable variance can create an adverse variance elsewhere;
• investigation should focus on material/significant variances;
• qualitative information is necessary for meaningful decisions.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 4 — Budgeting and Budgetary Control
content:
BUDGETING

A budget is a quantified plan for a future period. Budgetary control compares planned results with actual or flexed results and investigates significant differences.

IMPORTANCE
Budgets help with:
• planning;
• coordination;
• resource allocation;
• cash management;
• target setting;
• performance evaluation;
• communication;
• early identification of problems.

BEHAVIOURAL ASPECTS
Budgets can motivate employees when targets are realistic and understood. Poorly designed budgets can cause dysfunctional behaviour, excessive pressure, budgetary slack or manipulation.

BUDGETS IN THE SYLLABUS

SALES BUDGET
Units expected to be sold × selling price = sales value.

PRODUCTION BUDGET
Production units = Sales units + Closing inventory of finished goods − Opening inventory of finished goods.

PURCHASES BUDGET
Units to purchase = Production/material requirement + Closing raw-material inventory − Opening raw-material inventory.

Then multiply units by expected unit cost to obtain value.

CASH BUDGET
Shows expected cash receipts and cash payments over time.

Opening cash
+ receipts
− payments
= closing cash.

A negative closing cash balance indicates a financing requirement/overdraft where appropriate.

MASTER BUDGET
A master budget combines functional budgets to present an overall plan.

LIMITING FACTORS
A limiting factor restricts the level of activity, such as:
• sales demand;
• labour hours;
• machine hours;
• raw materials;
• finance;
• production capacity.

The limiting factor should be identified before preparing a realistic budget.

FLEXED BUDGET
A flexed budget adjusts budgeted costs/revenues to the actual level of activity, allowing a fairer comparison with actual performance.

For a variable cost:
Flexed cost = Budgeted variable cost per unit × actual activity.

Fixed cost normally remains unchanged within the relevant range.

CAUSES OF DIFFERENCES BETWEEN ACTUAL AND FLEXED BUDGET
• price changes;
• efficiency changes;
• changes in output;
• waste;
• supplier changes;
• unexpected repairs;
• staffing changes;
• changes in sales mix.

BUDGETARY CONTROL PROCESS
1. Set objectives.
2. Prepare budgets.
3. Communicate responsibilities.
4. Record actual results.
5. Flex the budget where necessary.
6. Compare actual with flexed budget.
7. Investigate significant variances.
8. Take corrective action.
9. Review future budgets.

EXAM TIP
Never compare an actual cost at one activity level with an unflexed variable-cost budget prepared for another activity level and then call the entire difference an efficiency problem.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 4 — Investment Appraisal: ARR, Payback, NPV and IRR
content:
INVESTMENT APPRAISAL

Investment appraisal evaluates whether a proposed long-term investment is financially worthwhile.

The syllabus includes:
• Accounting Rate of Return (ARR);
• Payback Period;
• Net Present Value (NPV);
• Internal Rate of Return (IRR);
• advantages and disadvantages of the techniques.

ACCOUNTING RATE OF RETURN

A common formulation is:
ARR = Average annual accounting profit / Average investment × 100.

Some questions may specify a different denominator convention, so use the formula given or the convention taught by the question.

Decision rule:
Higher ARR is generally preferred, provided it exceeds the required target rate.

ADVANTAGES
• uses accounting profit;
• relatively simple;
• easy to communicate.

LIMITATIONS
• ignores the time value of money;
• affected by depreciation/accounting policy;
• does not directly measure cash flows.

PAYBACK PERIOD

Payback measures the time required to recover the initial investment from project cash inflows.

If annual cash flows are equal:
Payback = Initial investment / Annual cash inflow.

If uneven:
accumulate cash inflows until the original investment is recovered.

Fractional year:
Unrecovered amount / cash inflow in the following period.

Advantages:
• simple;
• emphasises liquidity;
• useful where rapid recovery matters.

Limitations:
• ignores cash flows after payback;
• usually ignores time value of money;
• may favour short projects even when long-term returns are better.

NET PRESENT VALUE

NPV recognises the time value of money.

Present value = Future cash flow × Discount factor.

NPV = Present value of future cash inflows − Present value of future cash outflows.

If initial investment occurs immediately:
NPV = Total PV of future net cash flows − Initial investment.

Decision rule:
• positive NPV → generally accept if independent and assumptions hold;
• negative NPV → generally reject;
• for mutually exclusive projects, the higher positive NPV is generally preferred.

DISCOUNT FACTOR
DF = 1 / (1 + r)^n
where r is the discount rate and n is the period.

Example at 10%:
Year 1 DF ≈ 0.9091
Year 2 DF ≈ 0.8264
Year 3 DF ≈ 0.7513.

INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN

IRR is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero.

Where two discount rates produce NPVs of opposite signs, interpolation can estimate IRR:

IRR ≈ Lower rate + [NPV at lower rate / (NPV at lower rate − NPV at higher rate)] × (Difference between rates).

The closer the two trial rates and the more linear the NPV relationship over that interval, the more useful the interpolation estimate.

DECISION RULE
Accept when IRR exceeds the required rate of return, subject to project constraints.

COMPARISON
ARR → accounting profit; simple; ignores time value.
Payback → speed of recovery; simple; ignores later returns.
NPV → wealth/value measure; considers time value; more calculation.
IRR → percentage return; considers time value; can be difficult with unusual cash flows.

EXAM METHOD
1. Write the cash-flow timeline.
2. Separate initial investment from future cash flows.
3. Apply the correct discount factor.
4. Calculate present values.
5. Sum and subtract initial investment.
6. State the decision.
7. Add qualitative considerations if asked.

QUALITATIVE FACTORS
Consider strategic fit, environmental effects, staff impact, reliability, risk, capacity, technology, market demand and availability of finance. A project should not be accepted solely because one numerical technique gives a favourable result.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — Cash Flow Statements, Notes, Directors' and Auditors' Reports
content:
STATEMENT OF CASH FLOWS

Cash flow reporting focuses on movements in cash and cash equivalents rather than accounting profit.

OPERATING ACTIVITIES
Examples include cash generated from the main revenue-producing activities.

INVESTING ACTIVITIES
Examples include purchase and disposal of property, plant and equipment and other qualifying investments.

FINANCING ACTIVITIES
Examples include issue of shares, borrowing, repayment of borrowings and relevant distributions.

WHY PROFIT DIFFERS FROM CASH
Profit includes non-cash expenses such as depreciation and may include accruals. It also reflects credit transactions. Cash flow records actual cash movements.

INDIRECT RECONCILIATION LOGIC
Start with the relevant profit measure.
Adjust for non-cash items.
Adjust for working-capital movements.
Remove items classified outside operating activities as required.
Arrive at operating cash flow before/after relevant tax/interest treatment according to the question's framework.

WORKING CAPITAL MOVEMENTS
Increase in receivables → usually reduces operating cash flow.
Increase in inventory → usually reduces operating cash flow.
Increase in payables → usually increases operating cash flow.
These are cash-flow effects of changes in working capital.

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
Notes provide additional detail that supports the primary statements, such as:
• accounting policies;
• detailed asset classes;
• share capital;
• borrowings;
• commitments;
• contingencies;
• significant estimates and judgements;
• other disclosures required by the reporting framework.

DIRECTORS' REPORT
A directors' report communicates important information about the company's affairs and performance as required by the applicable framework/company requirements.

AUDITOR'S REPORT
An audit report communicates the auditor's opinion on whether the financial statements have been prepared/presented in accordance with the applicable reporting framework and whether they are materially misstated, within the scope of the audit.

IMPORTANT DISTINCTION
Management prepares the financial statements. The independent auditor examines evidence and expresses an audit opinion. The auditor does not guarantee that fraud or every error has been found.

FINANCIAL REPORTING USERS
Use cash flow information alongside profitability, liquidity, solvency and efficiency ratios. A profitable business can still fail if it cannot meet cash obligations.

EXAM TIP
If asked to explain why a company with high profit has cash problems, discuss receivables, inventory, capital expenditure, debt repayment, working-capital movements and timing rather than simply saying “profit is not cash.”

subject: Accounting
topic: Accounting A-Level — Integrated Worked Methods and Exam Checklist
content:
INTEGRATED WORKED METHOD 1 — PROFIT ADJUSTMENT

Suppose:
Revenue = $120,000
Opening inventory = $20,000
Purchases = $65,000
Closing inventory = $25,000
Operating expenses before adjustments = $18,000
Accrued expense at year end = $2,000
Prepaid expense at year end = $1,000

Cost of sales = 20,000 + 65,000 − 25,000 = $60,000.
Gross profit = 120,000 − 60,000 = $60,000.

If the $18,000 expense includes the amount paid before adjustment:
Adjusted expense = 18,000 + closing accrual 2,000 − closing prepayment 1,000 = $19,000.

Profit before other adjustments = $41,000.

The method matters: inventory determines cost of sales; accruals and prepayments determine the expense belonging to the period.

INTEGRATED WORKED METHOD 2 — BREAK-EVEN

Selling price = $80
Variable cost = $50
Fixed cost = $90,000

Contribution = $30 per unit.
Break-even units = 90,000 / 30 = 3,000 units.

At 4,000 units:
Total contribution = 4,000 × 30 = $120,000.
Profit = 120,000 − 90,000 = $30,000.

Margin of safety = 4,000 − 3,000 = 1,000 units.

INTEGRATED WORKED METHOD 3 — FLEXED BUDGET

Suppose variable production cost is budgeted at $12 per unit and fixed production cost at $20,000. Original budget was 2,000 units but actual production is 2,500 units.

Original variable budget = 2,000 × 12 = $24,000.
Flexed variable budget = 2,500 × 12 = $30,000.
Flexed total budget = $30,000 + $20,000 = $50,000.

If actual cost is $53,000:
Variance against flexed budget = $3,000 adverse.

The $6,000 increase from original to flexed variable budget is not automatically an adverse variance; it is explained by the higher activity level.

INTEGRATED WORKED METHOD 4 — RATIO INTERPRETATION

If:
Gross profit rises from $40,000 to $45,000,
but revenue rises from $100,000 to $150,000,

Previous gross margin = 40%.
Current gross margin = 30%.

Although gross profit increased in absolute terms, profitability per dollar of revenue fell. A good interpretation therefore distinguishes absolute figures from ratios.

EXAM PRESENTATION CHECKLIST

Before submitting:
□ Read the requirement and identify the exact statement/account/decision requested.
□ Use headings and dates.
□ Show calculations.
□ Keep debit and credit entries clearly labelled.
□ Distinguish capital from revenue.
□ Apply accruals and prepayments.
□ Check inventory treatment.
□ Check depreciation and disposals.
□ Check control-account balances.
□ Label favourable/adverse variances.
□ State ratio formulas.
□ Interpret changes rather than merely calculating.
□ For budgets, identify the limiting factor.
□ For investment appraisal, state the decision rule.
□ Include qualitative factors when evaluation is requested.
□ Check arithmetic and the accounting equation.

COMMON MISTAKES
1. Confusing mark-up with margin.
2. Treating drawings as an expense.
3. Forgetting closing inventory.
4. Putting accruals/prepayments on the wrong side.
5. Treating depreciation as a cash payment.
6. Using profit instead of contribution in a marginal-costing decision.
7. Ignoring the limiting factor.
8. Calling every difference a variance without flexing for activity.
9. Calculating ratios without interpretation.
10. Selecting an investment solely from payback when NPV is required.
11. Forgetting the difference between ordinary share capital and loan capital.
12. Failing to distinguish accounting profit from cash flow.

FINAL REVISION STRATEGY
For each topic, practise three layers:
Layer 1 — Definitions and principles.
Layer 2 — Structured calculations and ledger/statement preparation.
Layer 3 — Interpretation, evaluation and decision making.

A strong A-Level Accounting candidate should be able to move from a transaction to ledger entries, from ledger balances to financial statements, and from financial statements to analysis and business decisions.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Advanced Company Workings and Statement Extracts
content:
COMPANY WORKING PAPER ROUTINE

For company questions, separate the problem into:
A. share capital;
B. share premium;
C. retained earnings/reserves;
D. loan notes and finance costs;
E. business acquisition;
F. statement extracts.

SHARE CAPITAL WORKING
Number of shares × nominal value = share capital.
Number of shares × issue price = cash proceeds.
Excess over nominal value = share premium where applicable.

Example:
100,000 ordinary shares of $1 nominal value issued at $1.40.
Share capital = $100,000.
Share premium = $40,000.
Bank = $140,000.

If a question includes issue expenses, do not automatically subtract them from the share capital figure. Follow the required accounting treatment and present the effect on the relevant reserve/cost as applicable.

BONUS ISSUE
If $50,000 of an eligible reserve is capitalised into share capital:
Dr relevant reserve $50,000
Cr share capital $50,000
No new cash is created by the bonus issue.

RIGHTS ISSUE
If existing shareholders are offered one new share for every five held at $1.20:
For 50,000 existing shares, new shares = 10,000.
Cash proceeds if fully subscribed = $12,000.

LOAN NOTE INTEREST
If loan notes of $200,000 carry 8% annual interest:
Annual finance cost = $16,000, subject to timing and any accrued amount.

BUSINESS ACQUISITION WORKING
Identifiable assets acquired = $X
Less liabilities assumed = $Y
Net identifiable assets = $X − $Y
Purchase consideration = $Z
Difference = goodwill or other relevant result.

If purchase consideration is $500,000 and net identifiable assets are $450,000:
Goodwill = $50,000.

POST-ACQUISITION POSITION
Only assets, liabilities and equity arising from the new company position should be included. Do not accidentally duplicate the seller's capital.

EQUITY PRESENTATION
A company statement of financial position may separate:
• ordinary share capital;
• preference share capital where relevant;
• share premium;
• retained earnings;
• other applicable reserves.

The exact headings should follow the question/framework.

EXAM TIP
Company questions reward orderly workings. Even if a final figure is wrong because of one arithmetic mistake, clear workings can make the error traceable and reduce cascading mistakes.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — Advanced Financial Statement Analysis and Decision Evaluation
content:
FINANCIAL ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK

A complete evaluation should consider four dimensions:

1. Profitability
Can the organisation generate adequate returns from its sales and resources?

2. Liquidity
Can it meet short-term obligations?

3. Efficiency/resource utilisation
How effectively are assets and working capital being used?

4. Financial risk/gearing
How much dependence is there on debt and how exposed is the organisation to finance costs and repayment pressure?

TREND ANALYSIS
Compare ratios across several years rather than relying on one period. A one-year improvement can be temporary.

PROFITABILITY DIAGNOSIS
If gross margin falls but net margin rises, investigate whether operating expenses have fallen significantly.
If gross margin rises but net margin falls, investigate operating expenses, finance costs or other charges.
If ROCE falls while profit rises, assets/capital employed may have increased faster than operating profit.

LIQUIDITY DIAGNOSIS
A falling current ratio can indicate increasing short-term pressure, but the reason matters.
A high current ratio may indicate excessive inventory or receivables rather than strong management.

RECEIVABLES
A longer collection period may indicate weak credit control or changes in customer terms. It can tie up cash and increase bad-debt risk.

INVENTORY
A falling inventory turnover may indicate slow-moving stock, overstocking or lower sales. A very high turnover can also be problematic if stock shortages disrupt sales.

PAYABLES
A longer payment period can preserve cash but may strain supplier relationships or cause loss of discounts.

GEARING
High gearing increases financial risk, especially where interest costs are fixed. However, debt can also support expansion and improve returns to shareholders when projects earn more than the cost of debt.

LIMITATIONS OF COMPARISON
Ratios can be distorted by:
• inflation;
• different accounting policies;
• seasonal businesses;
• acquisitions/disposals;
• unusual one-off items;
• different business models;
• changes in product mix.

EVALUATION SENTENCE STRUCTURE
“Ratio X changed from A to B, indicating ____. This may be caused by ____. The implication is ____. Management could respond by ____.”

This structure turns a calculation into analysis.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Double-Entry Transaction Drills
content:
TRANSACTION ANALYSIS DRILLS

The safest method is to identify what the business receives and what it gives up, then classify each item.

1. Owner introduces $30,000 cash.
Dr Bank/Cash $30,000
Cr Capital $30,000
Effect: asset increases; owner's equity increases.

2. Buy equipment for $8,000 cash.
Dr Equipment $8,000
Cr Bank $8,000
Effect: one asset increases and another decreases. No immediate expense merely because cash was paid.

3. Buy goods on credit for $5,000.
Dr Purchases/Inventory as required $5,000
Cr Trade payables $5,000.

4. Sell goods on credit for $7,500.
Dr Trade receivables $7,500
Cr Sales $7,500.
The cost of the goods sold must also be accounted for where a perpetual inventory system requires it.

5. Customer pays $4,000 by bank.
Dr Bank $4,000
Cr Trade receivables $4,000.

6. Pay supplier $3,000.
Dr Trade payables $3,000
Cr Bank $3,000.

7. Owner withdraws $1,000 cash.
Dr Drawings $1,000
Cr Bank $1,000.
Drawings reduce equity; they are not a business expense.

8. Pay wages $2,500.
Dr Wages $2,500
Cr Bank/Cash $2,500.

9. Accrue wages of $600 at year end.
Dr Wages expense $600
Cr Accrued wages/payable $600.

10. Pay $12,000 insurance for twelve months starting on 1 October.
If the year ends 31 December, current-period expense is $3,000 and the remaining $9,000 is a prepayment.
Dr Insurance expense $3,000
Dr Prepayment $9,000
Cr Bank $12,000.

CAPITAL VS REVENUE

Capital expenditure normally creates or improves a non-current asset. Revenue expenditure relates to the ordinary running of the business.

Example:
Buying a delivery vehicle → capital expenditure.
Fuel used by the vehicle → revenue expenditure.
Major expenditure that creates a qualifying improvement may require careful classification.

WHY MISCLASSIFICATION MATTERS
If capital expenditure is wrongly treated as revenue:
• current expenses are overstated;
• current profit is understated;
• non-current assets are understated.

If revenue expenditure is wrongly capitalised:
• current expenses are understated;
• current profit is overstated;
• assets may be overstated.

ACCOUNTING EQUATION CHECK
After every transaction, verify:
Assets = Equity + Liabilities.

This is an excellent self-check during structured questions.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Errors, Suspense Accounts and Correction Techniques
content:
ERROR CORRECTION METHOD

STEP 1: Determine the intended transaction.
STEP 2: Determine what was actually recorded.
STEP 3: Identify the missing, excess or wrongly classified amount.
STEP 4: Prepare the correcting journal entry.
STEP 5: Determine whether suspense is involved.
STEP 6: Recheck the trial balance.

ERROR OF OMISSION
A transaction is completely omitted.
Example: credit purchase of $2,000 not recorded.
Correction:
Dr Purchases $2,000
Cr Trade payables $2,000.

ERROR OF COMMISSION
The amount is posted to the wrong account within an appropriate category.
Example: a $700 credit sale to Customer A is posted to Customer B.
The sales account may still be correct and the trial balance may balance, but individual receivables are wrong.

ERROR OF PRINCIPLE
A capital item is treated as revenue or vice versa.
Example: machinery installation cost is wrongly debited to repairs expense.
Correction transfers the amount to the appropriate non-current asset account.

COMPLETE REVERSAL
A transaction intended as:
Dr Expense
Cr Bank
is entered:
Dr Bank
Cr Expense.
The correcting entry needs to reverse the incorrect effect and then restore the intended treatment.

COMPENSATING ERRORS
Two errors may cancel numerically. The trial balance can still agree.

SUSPENSE ACCOUNT EXAMPLE
Suppose the debit total exceeds the credit total by $1,200. A suspense credit of $1,200 may be inserted temporarily to make the trial balance agree.

If a later investigation finds that $1,200 of sales was omitted from the sales account:
Dr Suspense $1,200
Cr Sales $1,200.

The suspense account is then cleared for that error.

CORRECTION OF GROSS PROFIT
Errors affecting purchases, sales, opening inventory or closing inventory can affect gross profit.

Examples:
• purchases understated → cost of sales understated → gross profit overstated;
• sales understated → gross profit understated;
• closing inventory understated → cost of sales overstated → gross profit understated.

CORRECTION OF NET PROFIT
An error affecting an operating expense can change net profit without changing gross profit.

Example:
Office expense of $1,000 omitted:
Profit is overstated by $1,000 until corrected.

WORKING CAPITAL
Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities.

When an error affects a current asset or current liability, assess the effect on working capital as well as profit.

EXAM TIP
Never assume that “trial balance agrees” means “no errors exist.” Explain the type of error and why the trial balance is or is not affected.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Depreciation, Accumulated Depreciation and Asset Disposal
content:
DEPRECIATION

Depreciation allocates the depreciable amount of a non-current asset over its useful life.

Depreciable amount = Cost − Residual value.

STRAIGHT-LINE
Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) / Useful life.

Example:
Cost $60,000
Residual value $6,000
Useful life 6 years
Annual depreciation = (60,000−6,000)/6 = $9,000.

REDUCING BALANCE
Annual depreciation = Opening carrying amount × rate.

Example:
Asset carrying amount $50,000
Rate 20%
Year 1 depreciation = $10,000.
Closing carrying amount = $40,000.
Year 2 depreciation = $8,000.

CARRYING AMOUNT
Carrying amount = Cost − accumulated depreciation − accumulated impairment losses where applicable.

DISPOSAL

Example:
Cost = $40,000
Accumulated depreciation at disposal = $26,000
Carrying amount = $14,000
Disposal proceeds = $16,000
Profit on disposal = $2,000.

The asset is removed from the books:
Dr Disposal account with carrying amount-related transfer
Cr Asset account with cost
and the accumulated depreciation is cleared according to the required ledger method. Disposal proceeds are then recorded and the resulting profit/loss transferred.

PART-YEAR DEPRECIATION
If an asset is purchased or disposed of during the year, calculate depreciation for the period of use according to the question's convention.

REVALUATION/VALUATION
When a question involves a change in asset valuation, distinguish cost, accumulated depreciation, carrying amount and the relevant revaluation/measurement treatment. Do not simply replace the asset cost with a new figure without accounting for the corresponding accumulated amounts and equity effects where required.

DEPRECIATION VS CASH FLOW
Depreciation is a non-cash accounting allocation. It reduces accounting profit but does not itself cause cash to leave the business in the period of depreciation.

WHY DEPRECIATION MATTERS
It prevents the entire cost of a long-term asset from being treated as a single-period expense and helps match the asset's cost with periods benefiting from its use.

EXAM CHECK
If asked for:
• expense → depreciation charge;
• carrying amount → cost less accumulated depreciation/impairment;
• disposal profit → proceeds less carrying amount;
• cash flow → remember depreciation is non-cash and may require adjustment in an indirect cash-flow calculation.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Partnership Appropriation, Capital and Current Accounts
content:
PARTNERSHIP PROFIT

The partnership's trading profit is not automatically the amount finally credited to partners. Appropriation items are dealt with according to the partnership agreement.

Example:
Profit before appropriation = $100,000.
Partner A salary = $12,000.
Partner B salary = $8,000.
Interest on capital A = $3,000.
Interest on capital B = $2,000.
Residual profit-sharing ratio A:B = 3:2.

Total appropriations before residual = $25,000.
Residual profit = $75,000.
A's share = $45,000.
B's share = $30,000.

Total profit allocation:
A = salary 12,000 + interest 3,000 + share 45,000 = $60,000.
B = salary 8,000 + interest 2,000 + share 30,000 = $40,000.

INTEREST ON DRAWINGS
If the agreement charges interest on drawings, calculate it for the relevant period and record it as an appropriation according to the required treatment.

CAPITAL ACCOUNTS

Fixed capital system:
The capital account generally remains at the agreed capital amount, while a separate current account records drawings, salary, interest and profit share.

Fluctuating capital system:
Capital account itself may change for profit share, drawings, salary and other relevant movements.

CURRENT ACCOUNT
A credit balance normally represents an amount owed by the partnership to the partner.
A debit balance may represent an amount owed by the partner to the partnership.

PARTNER ADMISSION
Admission may require:
• goodwill;
• revaluation;
• capital contribution;
• revised profit-sharing ratio.

GOODWILL
If goodwill is recognised and then written off, the entries depend on the partnership agreement and the treatment required by the question.

REVALUATION
A revaluation account can record increases/decreases in assets and liabilities. The resulting gain/loss is generally allocated to existing partners in the pre-change ratio unless the question specifies otherwise.

DISSOLUTION
A dissolution question often combines:
• transfer of assets;
• transfer of liabilities;
• disposal proceeds;
• settlement expenses;
• realisation profit/loss;
• partners' capital accounts;
• final cash distribution.

EXAM METHOD
Draw a clear table of partners, ratios and capital/current accounts before starting calculations. This prevents a correct figure being allocated to the wrong partner.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Manufacturing Account Detailed Working
content:
MANUFACTURING COST STRUCTURE

DIRECT MATERIALS
Opening raw materials
+ purchases
+ carriage inwards where relevant
− returns outwards
− closing raw materials
= materials consumed.

DIRECT LABOUR
Include wages directly attributable to production.

DIRECT EXPENSES
Include directly traceable production expenditure.

PRIME COST
Direct materials consumed
+ direct labour
+ direct expenses
= prime cost.

FACTORY OVERHEAD
Examples:
• indirect materials;
• indirect labour;
• factory power;
• factory rent;
• factory depreciation;
• production supervision.

WORK-IN-PROGRESS
Opening work in progress is added.
Closing work in progress is deducted.

COST OF PRODUCTION
Prime cost
+ factory overhead
+ opening work in progress
− closing work in progress
= cost of production.

COST OF GOODS SOLD
For a manufacturing business that also holds finished goods:
Opening finished goods
+ cost of production
− closing finished goods
= cost of goods sold.

GROSS PROFIT
Sales
− cost of sales
= gross profit.

UNREALISED PROFIT
If finished goods are transferred to a trading department at a transfer price above production cost, closing stock can contain an unrealised profit element.

Example:
Production cost of unit = $80.
Transfer price = $100.
Profit element = $20.
If 300 units remain in closing inventory:
Unrealised profit = $20 × 300 = $6,000.

The unrealised profit should not be treated as earned by the business as a whole until the goods are sold externally.

DEPARTMENTAL AND MANUFACTURING LINK
A business may have production, administration and selling departments. Production overhead belongs in manufacturing cost, while administration/selling costs are normally dealt with outside manufacturing cost.

EXAM CHECK
Keep:
• raw materials;
• work in progress;
• finished goods;
• factory overhead;
• selling/administration overhead
separate. Mixing these stages is a common cause of wrong cost of sales.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Not-for-Profit Organisations Detailed Working
content:
NOT-FOR-PROFIT ACCOUNTING

A not-for-profit organisation exists primarily to provide services or achieve a social/community purpose rather than distribute profit to owners.

KEY STATEMENTS
1. Receipts and payments account — records cash/bank receipts and payments.
2. Income and expenditure account — determines surplus/deficit for the period.
3. Statement of financial position — shows assets, liabilities and accumulated fund.

RECEIPTS AND PAYMENTS
This is primarily cash-based. It can include capital and revenue items.

INCOME AND EXPENDITURE
This is accrual-based. Only income and expenditure relating to the period are included.

SUBSCRIPTIONS
Example:
Cash received = $18,000
Opening arrears = $1,500
Closing arrears = $2,000
Opening advance = $800
Closing advance = $1,200

Subscription income:
18,000 + 2,000 − 1,500 + 800 − 1,200
= $18,100.

ACCUMULATED FUND
Opening accumulated fund may be obtained by preparing an opening statement of financial position:
Opening accumulated fund = Opening assets − Opening liabilities.

CAPITAL RECEIPTS
Examples can include donations specifically intended for capital purposes, legacies or proceeds from sale of non-current assets. Classification depends on the terms and facts.

SPECIAL FUNDS
Where money is restricted for a particular purpose, it should not automatically be treated as unrestricted general income.

INCOME-GENERATING EVENTS
For a dinner, raffle or dance:
Sales/receipts
− direct costs
= surplus from the activity.

If inventory is purchased for resale at an event, determine the cost of goods actually consumed/sold rather than treating all purchases as current-period expense when the accounting basis requires inventory adjustment.

EXAM TIP
Start with a classification table:
Cash item | Capital/revenue | Accrual adjustment | Final statement.
This greatly reduces errors.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — IAS 2 and IAS 16 Applied Calculations
content:
IAS 2 INVENTORIES — APPLICATION

Inventory cost may include:
• purchase price;
• import duties and non-recoverable taxes;
• transport and handling directly attributable to acquisition;
• conversion costs;
• other costs incurred in bringing inventory to present condition/location where applicable.

Costs that do not contribute to bringing inventory to its present condition/location are normally treated separately.

NRV
NRV = Estimated selling price − costs of completion − costs necessary to make the sale.

Example:
Expected selling price = $15,000
Completion costs = $1,200
Selling costs = $800
NRV = $13,000.

If cost is $14,500, inventory should be measured at the lower relevant amount, so the carrying amount becomes $13,000 and the $1,500 difference affects profit under the applicable treatment.

IAS 16 PPE — APPLIED LOGIC

Initial measurement includes appropriate costs necessary to bring the asset to the location and condition necessary for operation, subject to the standard's requirements.

Subsequent measurement can involve a cost model or revaluation model where applicable.

Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use under the relevant policy, not simply when management eventually starts using it.

Useful life and residual value should be reviewed where required.

COMPONENT ACCOUNTING
If significant components of an asset have different useful lives, they may require separate depreciation treatment under the applicable framework.

SUBSEQUENT EXPENDITURE
Routine repairs are generally expensed.
Expenditure that meets recognition criteria for a replacement/component or qualifying improvement may be capitalised.

DISPOSAL
Remove the asset's carrying amount and recognise the proceeds and resulting gain/loss.

EXAM WRITING
For an IAS question, state:
• recognition/measurement rule;
• calculation;
• financial-statement effect;
• any relevant disclosure/presentation point.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — IAS 7 Cash Flow Worked Structure
content:
CASH FLOW CLASSIFICATION

OPERATING
Cash received from customers.
Cash paid to suppliers.
Cash paid to employees.
Other operating receipts/payments.

INVESTING
Purchase of property, plant and equipment.
Proceeds from sale of property, plant and equipment.
Acquisition/disposal of relevant investments.

FINANCING
Issue of shares.
Borrowing proceeds.
Repayment of borrowings.
Relevant financing distributions/payments.

INDIRECT METHOD WORKING

Suppose:
Profit before tax = $80,000
Depreciation = $10,000
Increase in receivables = $6,000
Increase in inventory = $4,000
Increase in payables = $3,000
Operating cash before tax/interest adjustments:
80,000 + 10,000 − 6,000 − 4,000 + 3,000
= $83,000.

The logic:
• depreciation is added back because it reduced profit without using cash;
• increases in operating current assets usually consume cash;
• increases in operating current liabilities usually provide cash.

DIRECT VS INDIRECT
Direct presentation lists major classes of operating cash receipts/payments.
Indirect presentation reconciles profit to operating cash flow.

NON-CASH TRANSACTIONS
A transaction that does not involve cash should not be included as a cash flow merely because it changes assets or liabilities. It may require separate disclosure.

CASH FLOW INTERPRETATION
Positive operating cash flow is generally desirable, but a single positive figure does not prove financial strength. Consider:
• capital expenditure;
• financing dependence;
• debt repayment;
• working capital;
• cash reserves.

EXAM TRAP
Do not add an increase in receivables. If customers owe more at year end, some reported revenue has not yet been collected in cash, so the increase normally reduces operating cash flow under the indirect method.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — Ratio Calculation Drills and Interpretation
content:
RATIO DRILL

Data:
Revenue = $500,000
Gross profit = $175,000
Operating profit = $80,000
Current assets = $120,000
Inventory = $45,000
Current liabilities = $60,000
Trade receivables = $50,000
Credit sales = $400,000
Trade payables = $36,000
Credit purchases = $300,000
Cost of sales = $325,000
Average inventory = $50,000
Capital employed = $400,000.

Gross margin:
175,000 / 500,000 × 100 = 35%.

Operating/net margin using the supplied operating-profit figure:
80,000 / 500,000 × 100 = 16%.

Current ratio:
120,000 / 60,000 = 2:1.

Quick ratio:
(120,000 − 45,000) / 60,000
= 1.25:1.

Receivables collection:
50,000 / 400,000 × 365 ≈ 45.6 days.

Payables payment:
36,000 / 300,000 × 365 ≈ 43.8 days.

Inventory turnover:
325,000 / 50,000 = 6.5 times.

ROCE:
80,000 / 400,000 × 100 = 20%.

INTERPRETATION
A 35% gross margin means 35 cents of gross profit is generated for each dollar of revenue before operating costs and other relevant charges.

A quick ratio of 1.25:1 means the business has $1.25 of quick assets for each $1 of current liabilities under the formula used.

A receivables period of about 46 days should be compared with the business's credit terms. If customers are supposed to pay in 30 days, the result may indicate collection problems.

A payables period of about 44 days may support cash management but should be compared with agreed supplier terms.

A turnover of 6.5 times means average inventory is represented in cost of sales approximately 6.5 times over the period.

EVALUATION
Never conclude “good” or “bad” solely from a textbook benchmark. Compare:
• prior years;
• industry norms;
• budgets;
• credit terms;
• business strategy.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — Cost Classification and Overhead Allocation Drill
content:
COST CLASSIFICATION

Direct material:
Raw material physically traceable to the product.

Indirect material:
Consumables used in production but not economically traced to individual units.

Direct labour:
Workers directly producing the goods.

Indirect labour:
Supervisors, cleaners or maintenance staff whose labour supports production rather than being traced directly to a single product.

Direct expense:
A directly attributable expense other than direct material/labour.

PRODUCTION OVERHEAD
Indirect production costs.

ADMINISTRATION OVERHEAD
Costs of general administration.

SELLING/DISTRIBUTION OVERHEAD
Costs of marketing, selling and delivering products.

APPORTIONMENT BASES

Rent/floor space → floor area.
Electricity → usage/meters or an appropriate activity basis.
Supervision → number of employees or direct labour where justified.
Machine maintenance → machine hours.
Insurance of equipment → asset value.
Canteen cost → number of employees.
Do not use a basis simply because it is easy; choose one that reflects cost causation.

OVERHEAD ANALYSIS SHEET
A typical process:
1. List overheads.
2. Allocate directly attributable overheads.
3. Apportion common overheads.
4. Total each production/service cost centre.
5. Re-apportion service cost centres where required.
6. Calculate OAR for production centres.
7. Absorb overhead into products/jobs.

SERVICE COST CENTRES
A service department supports production. Its cost may need to be re-apportioned to production departments before calculating final absorption rates.

OVERHEAD ABSORPTION EXAMPLE
Budgeted factory overhead = $180,000.
Budgeted machine hours = 30,000.
OAR = $6 per machine hour.

Job X uses 120 machine hours:
Overhead absorbed = $720.

If actual overhead incurred is $185,000 and actual machine hours are 31,000:
Absorbed overhead = 31,000 × $6 = $186,000.
Over-absorption = $1,000.

EXAM TIP
Do not calculate OAR from actual overhead if the question asks for a predetermined/budgeted rate.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — CVP and Short-Run Decision Cases
content:
SPECIAL ORDER

A business has spare capacity.
Selling price for special order = $28.
Variable cost = $20.
Additional fixed cost = $0.

Contribution = $8 per unit.

If 5,000 units are accepted:
Additional contribution = $40,000.

If the order requires overtime or special packaging, include those incremental costs. If accepting it displaces normal sales, include the opportunity cost of lost contribution.

MAKE OR BUY

Compare relevant costs, not sunk costs.

If making internally:
Variable production cost = $15/unit.
Avoidable fixed cost = $3/unit.
Relevant make cost = $18/unit.

Supplier price = $20/unit.
Making saves $2/unit, assuming quality, capacity and strategic factors are acceptable.

If fixed cost cannot be avoided, it is irrelevant to the short-run comparison.

DISCONTINUING A PRODUCT

Do not discontinue a product simply because it shows an accounting loss after allocated fixed costs.

Example:
Product contribution = $30,000.
Allocated fixed cost = $45,000.
Reported loss = $15,000.

If all $45,000 fixed costs remain after discontinuation, removing the product reduces total profit by $30,000. If $20,000 of fixed cost is avoidable, discontinuation effect is:
Lost contribution $30,000
− fixed cost saved $20,000
= $10,000 reduction in profit.
Therefore the product should normally be retained financially, subject to qualitative considerations.

LIMITING FACTOR

Product A contribution = $18, requires 3 machine hours.
Contribution per machine hour = $6.

Product B contribution = $20, requires 2 machine hours.
Contribution per machine hour = $10.

If machine hours are scarce, B has priority, subject to demand and other constraints.

MULTIPLE LIMITING FACTORS
Use linear programming or other appropriate optimisation methods only if the question requires them. At basic level, identify the scarce resource and rank by contribution per unit of that resource.

QUALITATIVE FACTORS
Consider:
• customer relationships;
• employee morale;
• quality;
• legal obligations;
• environmental effects;
• long-term pricing;
• competitor response;
• brand reputation.

A purely numerical answer can be incomplete where evaluation is required.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 — Standard Costing Detailed Variance Interpretation
content:
MATERIAL VARIANCE ANALYSIS

Suppose standard for actual output is 2,000 kg at $5/kg.
Actual usage = 2,200 kg at $5.50/kg.

Material price variance:
(5.00 − 5.50) × 2,200
= $1,100 adverse.

Material usage variance:
(2,000 − 2,200) × 5.00
= $1,000 adverse.

Total material cost variance = $2,100 adverse.

Interpretation:
The price variance may result from supplier price increases or poor purchasing terms.
The usage variance may result from waste, defective material, poor handling, production inefficiency or a deliberate substitution decision.

LABOUR EXAMPLE

Standard hours for output = 4,000 hours.
Standard rate = $10/hour.
Actual hours = 4,200.
Actual rate = $10.50/hour.

Rate variance:
(10 − 10.50) × 4,200
= $2,100 adverse.

Efficiency variance:
(4,000 − 4,200) × 10
= $2,000 adverse.

Total labour cost variance = $4,100 adverse.

FAVOURABLE PRICE + ADVERSE USAGE
Suppose cheaper material creates a favourable price variance but causes more waste. The two variances should be investigated together. A purchasing department may achieve a favourable price result while production experiences an adverse usage result.

SALES PRICE VARIANCE
Actual sales quantity × (Actual selling price − Standard selling price).

If actual quantity = 10,000 units, actual price = $12 and standard price = $11:
Variance = 10,000 × 1 = $10,000 favourable.

SALES VOLUME
If standard contribution is $4/unit and actual sales exceed standard sales by 2,000 units:
Sales volume contribution variance = 2,000 × $4 = $8,000 favourable, subject to the exact convention required.

VARIANCE RECONCILIATION
Use a bridge:
Standard/budgeted profit
+ favourable variances
− adverse variances
= actual profit.

MANAGEMENT RESPONSE
A variance should trigger investigation when it is:
• large;
• persistent;
• unusual;
• controllable;
• strategically important.

Not every variance is worth investigating. Investigation itself has a cost.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 4 — Sales, Production, Purchases, Cash and Master Budgets
content:
BUDGET SEQUENCE

A common sequence is:
Sales budget
→ Production budget
→ Materials usage/purchases budget
→ Labour budget
→ Overhead budget
→ Cash budget
→ Budgeted income statement/statement of financial position where required.

SALES
Expected sales volume × expected selling price.

PRODUCTION
Expected sales
+ desired closing finished goods
− opening finished goods
= required production.

MATERIAL USAGE
Production units × material per unit.

MATERIAL PURCHASES
Material required for production
+ desired closing raw-material inventory
− opening raw-material inventory
= purchases.

LABOUR
Units produced × labour hours per unit × labour rate.

CASH BUDGET
Opening cash
+ cash receipts
− cash payments
= closing cash.

CREDIT SALES
Do not put the full credit sale into cash in the same month unless the collection terms say so. Build a collection pattern.

Example:
January credit sales $40,000.
60% collected in month of sale, 40% next month.
January cash from January credit sales = $24,000.
February cash from January credit sales = $16,000.

CASH PURCHASES
Similarly, cash payments depend on supplier credit terms.

MASTER BUDGET
Combines functional budgets and provides an overall plan.

BUDGETARY SLACK
Managers may deliberately understate expected revenue or overstate expected costs to make targets easier. Effective controls reduce dysfunctional slack while keeping targets realistic.

PARTICIPATIVE BUDGETING
Involving managers/employees can improve ownership and information quality, but can also increase negotiation and slack.

TOP-DOWN VS BOTTOM-UP
Top-down budgets are set mainly by senior management.
Bottom-up/participative budgets involve operational managers.

LIMITING FACTOR
The principal budget factor determines the maximum feasible activity. It must be identified before finalising production and related budgets.

EXAM TIP
Draw a month-by-month table when timing matters. Most cash-budget mistakes are timing errors rather than arithmetic errors.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 4 — Investment Appraisal Numerical Drill
content:
PROJECT DATA
Initial investment = $100,000.
Year 1 cash inflow = $40,000.
Year 2 = $45,000.
Year 3 = $35,000.
Discount rate = 10%.

Approximate discount factors:
Year 1 = 0.9091
Year 2 = 0.8264
Year 3 = 0.7513.

Present values:
Year 1 = 40,000 × 0.9091 = $36,364.
Year 2 = 45,000 × 0.8264 = $37,188.
Year 3 = 35,000 × 0.7513 = $26,296.

Total PV ≈ $99,848.
NPV ≈ $99,848 − $100,000 = −$152.

The result is approximately break-even at a 10% discount rate, but slightly negative under these rounded figures.

PAYBACK
Cumulative:
Year 1 = $40,000.
Year 2 = $85,000.
Remaining = $15,000.
Year 3 inflow = $35,000.
Fraction of year 3 = 15,000 / 35,000 ≈ 0.429.
Payback ≈ 2.43 years.

ARR
If average annual accounting profit were supplied, divide it by the specified average investment base and multiply by 100. Do not substitute cash flow for accounting profit unless the question's formula explicitly instructs it.

IRR
If NPV at 8% is positive and NPV at 12% is negative, the IRR lies between 8% and 12%. Interpolate using the two NPVs.

INVESTMENT APPRAISAL COMPARISON
A project can have:
• short payback but low NPV;
• high ARR but low cash generation;
• high IRR but lower NPV than another mutually exclusive project.

Therefore the decision technique matters.

NPV is often especially useful because it measures value created at the chosen discount rate, but the final choice should follow the requirement and assumptions of the question.

EXAM CHECK
Always write the initial investment as a time-zero cash flow. Do not discount time-zero cash.

subject: Accounting
topic: Accounting A-Level — High-Value Practice Questions and Marking Focus
content:
PRACTICE SET A — FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING

Question 1:
A sole proprietor has opening capital of $70,000, closing capital of $92,000, drawings of $15,000 and additional capital introduced of $8,000.
Calculate profit.

Method:
Profit = Closing capital + drawings − additional capital − opening capital.
= 92,000 + 15,000 − 8,000 − 70,000
= $29,000.

Question 2:
An expense paid is $10,000. Opening accrual is $1,200 and closing accrual is $1,700. Opening prepayment is $500 and closing prepayment is $300.
Calculate expense for the period:
10,000 + 1,700 − 1,200 + 500 − 300
= $10,700.

PRACTICE SET B — FINANCIAL REPORTING

Question:
Revenue $300,000; gross profit $90,000; operating profit $36,000.
Calculate gross margin and operating margin.
Gross margin = 90,000/300,000 ×100 = 30%.
Operating margin = 36,000/300,000 ×100 = 12%.

Then explain two possible reasons why operating margin could fall while gross margin remains unchanged:
• operating expenses increased;
• administrative/selling costs increased;
• finance-related or other relevant charges increased depending on the profit measure.

PRACTICE SET C — COST ACCOUNTING

Question:
Fixed costs $75,000; selling price $40; variable cost $25.
Contribution = $15.
Break-even = 75,000/15 = 5,000 units.
Target profit $30,000:
(75,000+30,000)/15 = 7,000 units.

PRACTICE SET D — BUDGETING

Question:
Budgeted production 10,000 units, variable cost $7/unit, fixed cost $30,000. Actual production 12,000 units. Actual total cost $120,000.
Flexed budget = (12,000×7)+30,000 = $114,000.
Variance = $6,000 adverse.

PRACTICE SET E — INVESTMENT APPRAISAL

Question:
Investment $80,000; annual cash inflows $25,000 for four years.
Payback = 80,000/25,000 = 3.2 years.
For NPV, obtain the specified discount factors and discount each year's inflow; subtract the $80,000 initial investment.

MARKING FOCUS
Markers reward:
• correct formula;
• substitution;
• arithmetic;
• units;
• working;
• appropriate conclusion;
• interpretation.

For “discuss” or “evaluate”, a calculation alone is insufficient. Explain benefits, limitations, causes and implications.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Integrated Financial Statement Adjustments
content:
YEAR-END ADJUSTMENT MASTER GUIDE

When a question gives a trial balance followed by adjustments, process the adjustments one at a time. Do not try to prepare the final statement directly from the trial balance without an adjustment schedule.

1. CLOSING INVENTORY
Closing inventory normally appears:
• in the statement of profit or loss calculation as a deduction from cost of sales;
• in the statement of financial position as a current asset.

2. ACCRUED EXPENSE
Add the closing accrual to the expense in profit or loss.
Show the accrual as a current liability.

3. PREPAID EXPENSE
Deduct the closing prepayment from the expense in profit or loss.
Show the prepayment as a current asset.

4. ACCRUED INCOME
Add the closing accrual to income.
Show the accrued income as a current asset.

5. INCOME RECEIVED IN ADVANCE
Deduct the closing advance from income.
Show the advance as a current liability.

6. DEPRECIATION
Calculate the current-period depreciation and charge it to the relevant expense/manufacturing section.
Increase accumulated depreciation.

7. DISPOSAL
Remove the original cost and accumulated depreciation of the disposed asset.
Record proceeds.
Calculate profit/loss on disposal.

8. BAD DEBTS
Remove confirmed irrecoverable receivables from trade receivables.
Charge the bad debt to profit or loss under the applicable treatment.

9. ALLOWANCE FOR DOUBTFUL DEBTS
Calculate the required closing allowance.
Compare it with the existing allowance.
The movement affects profit or loss.

10. INVENTORY WRITE-DOWN
If required by the IAS 2 treatment, reduce inventory to the lower relevant measurement and recognise the corresponding expense/loss.

11. LOAN INTEREST
Accrued interest belongs in the current period and creates a liability if unpaid.

12. DIVIDENDS
Do not treat dividends as operating expenses. They are distributions to owners and affect equity according to the applicable treatment.

13. TAX
Where tax is included in a question, calculate according to the stated rate and basis. Distinguish tax expense from tax payable.

14. CAPITAL EXPENDITURE
If an item was wrongly included in an expense account but is actually a qualifying non-current asset, correct the classification before finalising profit and assets.

ADJUSTMENT TABLE

Create a table:
Adjustment | Profit or loss effect | Statement of financial position effect.

Example:
Closing accrual → expense increases → current liability increases.
Closing prepayment → expense decreases → current asset increases.
Depreciation → expense increases → non-current asset carrying amount decreases.
Closing inventory → cost of sales decreases → current asset increases.

FINAL CONTROL
After all adjustments:
• check that assets = equity + liabilities;
• compare gross profit with the trading calculation;
• check current assets and current liabilities;
• ensure every adjustment has been reflected in all places where required.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 1 — Internal Control, Fraud Risk and Accounting Systems

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 2 — Reporting Concepts, Qualitative Information and Users
content:
QUALITATIVE CHARACTERISTICS

Useful financial information should possess qualities that make it useful for decision making.

RELEVANCE
Information is relevant when it can influence decisions by helping users evaluate past, present or future events or confirm/correct previous evaluations.

FAITHFUL REPRESENTATION
Information should represent the economic phenomena it purports to represent. It should be complete, neutral and as free from error as practical.

COMPARABILITY
Users should be able to identify similarities and differences between periods and entities.

VERIFIABILITY
Different knowledgeable observers should be able to reach reasonable agreement that the information faithfully represents the underlying phenomena.

TIMELINESS
Information should be available in time to influence decisions.

UNDERSTANDABILITY
Information should be classified, characterised and presented clearly.

MATERIALITY
An item is material if omitting, misstating or obscuring it could reasonably be expected to influence users' decisions.

ACCOUNTING POLICY VS ESTIMATE VS ERROR

Policy:
The specific principles, bases and rules used in preparing financial statements.

Estimate:
A monetary amount subject to measurement uncertainty, such as useful life or expected credit loss-type estimates.

Error:
An omission or misstatement caused by failure to use, or misuse of, available reliable information.

WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS
The treatment of a change depends on its nature. Do not automatically call every change a “policy change”.

USERS AND DECISIONS

Investors:
Should they invest, retain or sell?

Lenders:
Can the entity repay interest and principal?

Management:
How should resources be allocated?

Employees:
Is employment and remuneration sustainable?

Government:
Are regulations/taxes complied with?

Suppliers:
Will amounts owed be paid?

Customers:
Will the business continue supplying goods/services?

PUBLIC:
What are the wider economic, social and environmental effects?

LIMITATIONS OF FINANCIAL REPORTING
Financial statements:
• are largely historical;
• contain estimates;
• may not capture non-financial value;
• can be affected by accounting policies;
• may not fully reflect current market values;
• should be read together with other information.

EXAM TIP
When asked why a user needs a particular figure, link the figure to the decision the user is making.

subject: Accounting
topic: Topic 3 & 4 — Integrated Costing, Budgeting and Performance Control
content:
COST AND BUDGET INTEGRATION

Cost accounting and management accounting are closely linked.

Example:
A business budgets production of 20,000 units.
Variable production cost = $9/unit.
Fixed production overhead = $80,000.

Budgeted total production cost:
20,000 × 9 = $180,000 variable.
+ $80,000 fixed.
= $260,000.

Budgeted unit production cost under absorption:
$260,000 / 20,000 = $13 per unit.

If actual output is 24,000 units, a flexed variable budget uses:
24,000 × $9 = $216,000.
Fixed remains $80,000 within the relevant range.
Flexed production cost = $296,000.

If actual cost = $310,000:
Adverse variance = $14,000.

WHY FLEXING MATTERS
If the original budget of $260,000 were compared directly with $310,000, the $50,000 difference would contain:
• $36,000 explained by increased variable activity;
• $14,000 residual performance difference.
The flexed budget isolates the performance difference more fairly.

COST BEHAVIOUR AND DECISIONS

If variable cost per unit rises:
Contribution falls.
Break-even point rises.
Target-profit output rises.

If selling price rises while demand remains adequate:
Contribution rises.
Break-even point falls.
Profit rises at a given volume.

If fixed cost rises:
Break-even point rises.
But contribution per unit does not change if variable cost and price remain unchanged.

BUDGET CONTROL LOOP

Plan → Budget → Operate → Measure → Compare → Investigate → Correct → Re-plan.

FEEDBACK
Past variances can improve future standards and budgets. A variance is therefore not merely a score; it is information for future control.

RESPONSIBILITY CENTRES
A manager should ideally be evaluated on costs/revenues they can influence. Uncontrollable costs should be interpreted carefully.

CONTROLLABLE VS UNCONTROLLABLE
A department manager may control labour scheduling but not a centrally allocated head-office rent charge. Performance reports should distinguish the two where possible.

PERFORMANCE MEASURES
Financial:
• profit;
• contribution;
• cost variances;
• budget variances;
• return measures.

Non-financial:
• quality;
• delivery time;
• customer satisfaction;
• defect rates;
• staff turnover;
• production downtime.

A good management-control system combines financial and non-financial indicators.

topic: Accounting A-Level — Final Revision Bank: Definitions, Formulas and Decision Rules
content:
HIGH-VALUE DEFINITIONS

Accounting — systematic identification, measurement, recording, classification, summarisation, analysis and communication of financial information.

Asset — a resource controlled by an entity as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected.

Liability — a present obligation arising from past events whose settlement is expected to result in an outflow of resources.

Capital/equity — the residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

Revenue — income arising from the entity's ordinary activities, subject to the applicable framework.

Expense — decreases in economic benefits during the period in the form of outflows/depletions or incurrences of liabilities that reduce equity, excluding distributions to owners.

Working capital — current assets minus current liabilities.

Contribution — sales less variable cost.

Break-even — activity level at which total contribution equals fixed costs and profit is zero.

Opportunity cost — benefit sacrificed by choosing the next-best alternative.

Sunk cost — past cost that cannot be changed by a current decision.

Cost centre — a unit/location/function for which costs are collected.

Cost unit — unit of product/service to which costs are assigned.

Variance — difference between an actual result and a standard/budget result.

Budget — quantified plan for a future period.

NPV — present value of future cash flows less initial investment/cash outflow.

IRR — discount rate at which NPV is zero.

FORMULA BANK

Accounting equation:
Assets = Equity + Liabilities.

Working capital:
Current assets − current liabilities.

Gross profit:
Revenue − cost of sales.

Cost of sales:
Opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory, adjusted for relevant direct costs/returns.

Straight-line depreciation:
(Cost − residual value) / useful life.

Gross margin:
Gross profit / revenue × 100.

Net/operating margin:
Relevant profit / revenue × 100.

Current ratio:
Current assets / current liabilities.

Quick ratio:
(Current assets − inventory) / current liabilities.

Receivables period:
Trade receivables / credit sales × 365.

Payables period:
Trade payables / credit purchases × 365.

Inventory turnover:
Cost of sales / average inventory.

Contribution:
Sales − variable costs.

Contribution per unit:
Selling price − variable cost per unit.

Break-even units:
Fixed costs / contribution per unit.

Target-profit units:
(Fixed costs + target profit) / contribution per unit.

Margin of safety:
Actual/budgeted sales − break-even sales.

C/S ratio:
Contribution / sales × 100.

OAR:
Budgeted overhead / budgeted activity.

Flexed variable cost:
Variable cost per unit × actual activity.

NPV:
Σ(Cash flow × discount factor) − initial investment.

IRR interpolation:
Lower rate + [NPV at lower rate/(NPV at lower rate − NPV at higher rate)] × rate interval.

DECISION RULE BANK

Positive NPV → generally accept, subject to constraints.
IRR above required return → generally acceptable.
Shorter payback → faster recovery, but ignores later returns unless discounted payback is specified.
Higher ARR → generally preferred when the target and method are comparable.
Higher contribution per limiting factor → priority where that factor is scarce.
Lower relevant cost → preferred in make/buy decisions if quality and strategic factors are acceptable.

FINAL EXAM HABITS
• Show workings.
• Label units.
• Use the correct formula.
• Keep calculations in sequence.
• Interpret results.
• State assumptions.
• Check whether the question asks for profit, cash flow, contribution, cost or value.
• Read the requirement before beginning the calculation.
